# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: A Narrative Review of Clinical Evolution, Challenges, and Future Horizons

## Introduction: The Conception of Bioresorbable Scaffolds
Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has evolved significantly over the past decades, transitioning from plain balloon angioplasty to contemporary metallic drug-eluting stents (DES). However, permanent metallic implants carry long-term limitations, such as persistent caging of the vessel wall, chronic low-grade vascular inflammation, a lifelong risk of very late stent thrombosis (VLST), and the limitation of future coronary artery bypass grafting (CABG) options. To overcome these limitations, the paradigm of "vascular reparative therapy" was introduced through the development of fully bioresorbable vascular scaffolds (BVS). These temporary scaffolds are engineered to provide transient radial support and control drug elution during the early high-risk phase of acute recoil and restenosis. Following complete bioresorption, the native coronary vessel is theoretically restored to its natural vasomotion, allowing for positive adaptive remodeling and physiological shear stress.

Historically, the earliest clinical bioresorbable platform was the non-drug-eluting poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA) Igaki-Tamai scaffold evaluated in 2000 [1]. This pioneering platform paved the way for drug-eluting polymeric platforms, most notably the Absorb Everolimus-Eluting Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffold (Abbott Vascular) [2]. Early clinical trials, such as the ABSORB II [3] and the pivotal ABSORB III trial [4], demonstrated the early feasibility of polymeric BVS, showing non-inferior 1-year target lesion failure (TLF) rates compared to metallic second-generation everolimus-eluting stents (EES). These encouraging outcomes were replicated in regional cohorts, including ABSORB Japan [5] and ABSORB China [6]. Furthermore, BVS demonstrated favorable acute healing in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) cohorts in the ABSORB-STEMI TROFI II trial [7], while a patient-level pooled analysis of 1-year trial data supported early efficacy [8]. Observational registries, such as GHOST-EU, also suggested acceptable safety in real-world clinical practice [9], [10].

## Clinical Setbacks and Market Withdrawal
However, longer-term clinical data exposed critical safety signals. The 3-year outcomes of the ABSORB II trial revealed significantly higher rates of late scaffold thrombosis (ST) and impaired vasoreactivity in BVS-treated vessels compared to metallic EES [11]. This was compounded by the randomized AIDA trial, which was terminated early by its data safety monitoring board due to a fivefold increase in ST in the BVS cohort [12]. Comprehensive analyses confirmed that both early and late BVS thrombosis occurred at rates significantly higher than metallic DES [13]. Intracoronary imaging with optical coherence tomography (OCT) and intravascular ultrasound (IVUS) demonstrated that underexpansion, malapposition, and strut fracture were common mechanical triggers of ST [14]. Furthermore, the INVEST registry revealed that structural discontinuity and neoatherosclerosis during the advanced stages of polymer resorption were primary drivers of very late scaffold thrombosis (VLScT) [15].

Subsequent pooled patient-level meta-analyses at three years verified these safety concerns [16]. Although the blinded ABSORB IV trial attempted to mitigate these risks by using a biomarker-enriched acute coronary syndrome cohort and emphasizing optimized deployment techniques, it failed to show clinical superiority of BVS over EES at one year [17]. Long-term results from the ABSORB III trial [18] and pooled individual-patient-data meta-analyses at five years [19] confirmed that the excess risk of clinical events persisted until the point of complete resorption (approximately three years). Consequently, Abbott withdrew the Absorb BVS from the global market in 2017.

## Deployment Optimization: The "PSP" Protocol
To minimize these failures, an expert consensus panel formalized the "PSP" protocol: aggressive lesion **P**re-dilatation, accurate vessel **S**izing (preferably guided by intravascular imaging), and mandatory high-pressure **P**ost-dilatation [20]. Although strict PSP adherence mitigated ST risk, a joint task force of the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) and European Association of Percutaneous Cardiovascular Interventions (EAPCI) recommended that first-generation BVS should not be chosen over contemporary metallic DES in routine clinical practice [21]. This was reflected in the 2018 ESC/EACTS Guidelines on Myocardial Revascularization, which issued a Class III (Harm) recommendation against the routine clinical use of first-generation BVS [22].

## Next-Generation Scaffolds and Future Perspectives
To overcome polymer-related physical limitations (namely, thick 150 µm struts), research has pivoted toward thinner-strut platforms and alternative bioresorbable alloys. Bioresorbable magnesium-based metallic scaffolds (mBRS) have emerged as highly promising, offering superior radial strength and faster resorption (approximately 12 months). Following the PROGRESS-AMS [23] and BIOSOLVE-I [24] trials, the sirolimus-eluting second-generation magnesium scaffold (Magmaris) demonstrated stable safety and low late lumen loss in the BIOSOLVE-II trial [25]. Sustained safety was recently confirmed in the BIOSOLVE-IV registry, which showed low rates of TLF and ST at two years [26].

In parallel, polymer engineering has yielded thinner-strut PLLA platforms. The Fantom scaffold (REVA Medical), composed of a radiopaque desaminotyrosine-derived polycarbonate with 125 µm struts, exhibited low 5-year rates of major adverse events and no late ST in the FANTOM II trial [27]. Other thin-strut platforms include the 100-µm MeRes100 [28] and the 100–125 µm Firesorb [29] sirolimus-eluting scaffolds, which have shown favorable vascular healing and minimal thrombogenicity in early clinical trials. However, further research into long-term vascular healing and the resorption process remains crucial [30].

## Conclusion
Although first-generation bioresorbable vascular scaffolds suffered clinical setbacks, the concept of "leaving nothing behind" remains highly attractive. Adherence to optimized deployment protocols, combined with next-generation ultra-thin polymer and magnesium-based scaffolds, has successfully addressed early safety concerns. Future randomized controlled trials are awaited to determine if these advanced platforms can establish therapeutic equivalence or superiority over contemporary metallic drug-eluting stents.
